cards.headline: Boca Raton TLC Program Offers Summer Service Projects for South Florida Families
cards.teaser: B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program connects volunteers with hands-on service projects ranging from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking and literacy efforts.
cards.body:
B'nai Torah Congregation's TLC Program is offering South Florida families a range of hands-on service projects this summer, from food support and shoe donations to pantry stocking, literacy efforts and care for seniors. Led by Summer Faerman, the program connects volunteers of all ages with mitzvah opportunities, or meaningful good deeds, as part of the congregation's broader community outreach efforts.

 The TLC Program stands for Tzedakah, Learning and Chesed, and has made service a central part of synagogue life since 2012. The program provides a way for individuals and families to put Jewish values into action while helping people in need across South Florida. It addresses multiple community concerns including hunger, homelessness, literacy, elder care, vulnerable populations and special needs. Organizers emphasize that the projects are open to everyone in the community, not only members of B'nai Torah Congregation, with the goal of making service practical, welcoming and easy to begin.

 Participants can volunteer in various ways throughout the summer. Projects include making sandwiches, serving meals, collecting and cleaning shoes, stocking Little Free Pantries, preparing backpacks for back-to-school efforts, creating Bags of Hope and helping seniors with technology. Organizers plan to demonstrate volunteer projects such as wrapping presents, making flower arrangements, preparing sandwiches, collecting shoes and assembling supplies for people in need. The variety of options allows families to choose activities that match their interests and schedules.

 As summer continues, the TLC Program offers families a way to stay connected, teach children about giving back and support neighbors throughout South Florida. B'nai Torah Congregation says the program is built around the idea that small acts of service can strengthen the larger community. More information about the TLC Program is available through B'nai Torah Congregation's website.

hero.headline: Florida Attorney General threatens Catholic school scholarship funding over vaccine exemption policies
hero.teaser: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state la
hero.body:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is challenging the state's Catholic bishops, warning that church-run schools must honor parents' religious vaccine exemptions under state law or risk losing access to state scholarship funding. In a letter to Catholic school leaders, Uthmeier argues state law requires schools to accept religious vaccine exemptions even if church leaders disagree. He also cites Vatican teaching on individual conscience in making his case.

 The financial stakes are significant. More than 525,000 Florida students use state scholarship programs, including roughly 92 percent of Catholic school students. Uthmeier has warned that schools could lose access to those programs if they do not comply. Existing policies at some Catholic schools, including one in Orlando, state that vaccines are not against Catholic teaching and that allowing exemptions could endanger students and staff.

 The clash follows Governor Ron DeSantis' broader campaign against vaccine mandates. Lawmakers rejected proposals this year to eliminate Florida's remaining school vaccine requirements or create a broader conscience exemption. Medical and religious opt-outs remain available.

 The Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops has not yet answered the argument directly. Michele Taylor of the Florida Conference of Catholic Bishops said the organization is reviewing the letter and will respond to the Attorney General by his requested date of August 7.

 State Democrats are calling the attorney general's demands a distraction. Rep. Daryl Campbell, a Fort Lauderdale Democrat, pointed to what he called more pressing concerns facing Floridians.

 Campbell said affordability has been the crisis of this generation. The bishops have until Friday to respond to Uthmeier's letter. For now, his scholarship threat remains a warning, not a funding cutoff.

cards.headline: Florida judge orders rewrite of Amendment 3 ballot language, calling it biased and misleading
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge has ordered Florida to rewrite the ballot language for Amendment 3, a sweeping property-tax proposal, ruling that the Legislature's description is biased, inacc
cards.body:
A Leon County judge has ordered Florida to rewrite the ballot language for Amendment 3, a sweeping property-tax proposal, ruling that the Legislature's description is biased, inaccurate and misleading. Circuit Judge David Frank granted summary judgment to challengers Monday night, declared the current title and summary clearly and conclusively defective, and blocked Secretary of State Cord Byrd from placing that wording on the November ballot.

 Frank ordered Attorney General James Uthmeier to submit corrected language to the Department of State within 10 days. The decision does not remove Amendment 3 itself from the ballot. The judge stressed that the court is not deciding whether the property-tax plan is good policy, only whether voters are receiving a fair and accurate explanation before making that decision.

 Three consolidated lawsuits challenged the title Save Our Homes From Excessive Property Taxes and a summary promising to benefit taxpayers, protect small businesses, preserve core services and ensure fairness. Frank agreed that the title resembles campaign messaging more than a neutral description. The title is more akin to a political slogan, Frank wrote.

 It is not fair or neutral. It advocates a policy position: to stop excessive property taxes. The judge found the word save was designed to provoke an emotional response.

 He also ruled that invoking Save Our Homes could confuse voters because that name is already commonly associated with Florida's existing 3 percent cap on annual assessment increases for homesteaded property. Amendment 3 would not change that cap.

 Frank directed Uthmeier to remove the summary's opening declaration that the amendment benefits Florida taxpayers and four promotional taglines: Exempting homestead properties from taxation, Ensuring funding for core services, Protecting small businesses and Ensuring fairness for Florida residents. The judge found several additional problems with the description.

 The summary says the amendment would exempt the first $250,000 of a homestead's value when it takes effect in 2027. The proposal would actually set the exemption at $150,000 during 2027 before increasing it to $250,000 in 2028 and adjusting it for inflation beginning in 2029. The court also rejected language promising a schedule for full elimination of non-school homestead property taxes. The amendment would instead require lawmakers to establish a procedure through which cities and counties could increase the exemption up to a home's full assessed value.

 The Legislature approved Amendment 3 during a June special session called by Gov. Ron DeSantis. For people who establish permanent Florida residency by Dec. 31, the proposal would increase the non-school homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028.

 School district property taxes would remain unaffected. The measure would also reduce the assessment-growth cap for non-homestead property from 10 percent to 5 percent. Florida's Revenue Estimating Conference projected the quantifiable portions would reduce local property-tax collections by nearly $4.93 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year.

 The modeled recurring impact is approximately $11.83 billion annually. Amendment 3 requires support from at least 60 percent of voters to pass in November.

cards.headline: Florida Sheriffs Association warns homestead exemption ballot measure could lengthen law enforcement response times
cards.teaser: The statewide association says a November ballot measure to increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners could create longer law enforcement response times.
cards.body:
The Florida Sheriffs Association has entered the tax reform debate, raising concerns about a November ballot measure that would increase the homestead exemption and lower tax bills for homeowners. The association states it has significant concerns with the referendum, warning it could potentially create longer law enforcement response times. Former Martin County Sheriff William Snyder said the association's position carries weight, noting that Florida sheriffs are always moderate in their responses and tend to be very supportive of the governor, making their opposition to the governor in this case a clear signal.

 Snyder said he understands the frustration driving the push for tax relief but warned the savings may come with hidden costs. He explained that instead of paying for services out of their left pocket, taxpayers will pay for it out of their right pocket, as sheriffs' offices and fire departments would look to other taxes and fees to make up the difference. Snyder served as Martin County sheriff for 12 years and managed the department's budgets throughout that time.

 Snyder said his department looked at every single nickel and could shave a little off the edges, but when 80 percent of the budget is personnel services, unless deputies or firefighters are let go, there is not much that can be done with the budget. The debate over cutting taxes and its impact on public safety is central to the amendment question facing voters in November. County and city leaders are grappling with how they would manage significant cuts in revenue as homeowners look to Tallahassee for relief from high tax bills.

cards.headline: Honduran national convicted in Fort Pierce federal court for firearms trafficking to Honduras
cards.teaser: A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them
cards.body:
A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them to Honduras. Luis Matute Figueroa, 33, of Lake Worth, was found guilty of conspiracy and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Monday.

 Matute Figueroa overstayed a tourist visa in 2017 and remained in the United States without lawful status. WhatsApp messages recovered during the investigation showed that Matute Figueroa provided co-conspirators with firearm inventories, pricing information and shipping instructions for weapons destined for Honduras. The messages also contained a photograph and a video of Matute Figueroa in possession of a distinctive gold Colt 1911 pistol. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe said the defendant exploited his unlawful presence in the United States to help traffic American firearms to Honduras.

 Court records and trial evidence showed that Matute Figueroa conspired with Gerson Eliu Padilla-Figueroa, Juan Matute Figueroa, Ariel Henriquez-Padilla, and William Mendoza to acquire firearms in the United States through straw purchases and illegally export them to Honduras. Straw purchases involve using individuals with clean records to buy firearms on behalf of those prohibited from owning them.

 Matute Figueroa faces up to five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count and up to 15 years in prison on the firearm possession count. A federal district court judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The ATF Miami Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations Miami investigated the case with assistance from the Broward Sheriff's Office, the Martin County Sheriff's Office, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Attorney Suzanne Huyler is prosecuting the case.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers sworn in as chairman of Florida Sheriffs Association
cards.teaser: Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. F
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers was sworn in Thursday as chairman of the Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors, succeeding his role as vice chairman last year. Flowers now leads the statewide organization that brings together sheriffs from across Florida to develop strategies for leading their counties.

 The Florida Sheriffs Association board of directors includes sheriffs from throughout the state who work together on law enforcement strategies and leadership issues affecting county agencies. Flowers served as vice chairman of the board during the previous year before taking on the chairmanship role.

 The swearing-in ceremony took place Thursday, marking Flowers' elevation to the top position in the statewide law enforcement organization. The association serves as a platform for sheriffs to collaborate on policies and approaches to county law enforcement challenges.

 Flowers continues to serve as sheriff of Indian River County while taking on the additional responsibilities of chairing the Florida Sheriffs Association board. The organization coordinates efforts among the state's 67 elected sheriffs on issues ranging from training standards to legislative priorities.

cards.headline: Postal worker arrested for stealing winning Florida Lottery ticket from mail in Miami
cards.teaser: A United States Postal Service letter carrier was arrested July 23 on charges of stealing a winning Pick 4 lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize. Lekaysh
cards.body:
A United States Postal Service letter carrier was arrested July 23 on charges of stealing a winning Pick 4 lottery ticket from the mail and fraudulently claiming the prize. Lekaysha Lockhart, who worked as a USPS letter carrier, faces charges including grand theft, dealing in stolen property, filing a false claim for payment, two counts of unlawful use of a two-way communications device and mail theft.

 The arrest followed a joint investigation by the Florida Lottery Division of Security and the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General. A Florida Lottery player reported that a winning Pick 4 ticket she mailed never reached its intended destination. A Florida Lottery Inspector determined the ticket had been redeemed by Lockhart on June 19 at the Florida Lottery's Miami District Office.

 Following her arrest, Florida Lottery Special Agents and USPS OIG investigators said Lockhart admitted to stealing the winning lottery ticket and redeeming it. Florida Lottery Secretary Reginald D. Dixon said the case reflects the agency's commitment to player protection. Dixon commended the Division of Security for their investigative work and thanked partners at the United States Postal Service Office of Inspector General and the Broward County Sheriff's Office for their collaboration.

 Because the alleged offenses occurred in multiple judicial circuits, the cases will be prosecuted separately, the Florida Lottery Division of Security said. The Florida Lottery's Office of Communications released details of the arrest in a news release.

cards.headline: Byron Donalds holds commanding lead in Florida GOP governor's race with three weeks until primary
cards.teaser: U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds maintains a dominant position in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary with fewer than three weeks remaining before the Aug. 19 election, buoyed by Pre
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds maintains a dominant position in Florida's Republican gubernatorial primary with fewer than three weeks remaining before the Aug. 19 election, buoyed by President Donald Trump's endorsement, superior name recognition and a significant financial advantage over his three main rivals. A political committee supporting Donalds this week released a statewide television and digital ad centered on affordability, showing Donalds playing basketball with his sons while promising to cut property taxes, lower insurance rates and reduce housing costs.

 A public Cygnal survey conducted July 12-13 found Donalds leading with 43 percent, followed by investor James Fishback at 12 percent, Lt. Gov. Jay Collins at 11 percent and former House Speaker Paul Renner at 2 percent.

 Another 31 percent remained undecided. The survey included 500 likely Republican primary voters and had a margin of error of 4.38 percentage points. Collins' campaign released an internal poll this week showing a closer contest, with Donalds at 46 percent and Collins at 30 percent, though public polling has generally shown Collins much farther behind.

 Fishback won a courtroom victory this week after Leon County Circuit Judge David Frank rejected Collins' attempt to remove him from the ballot. Collins had pointed to Fishback's 2020 vote in Washington, D.C., his purchase of a condominium there and tax, mortgage and homestead records as evidence that Fishback had established residency outside Florida. Frank ruled that Collins failed to overcome Florida's legal presumptions favoring continued residency and candidate access to the ballot.

 Fishback responded by calling on Collins to resign as lieutenant governor, calling the legal challenge an attempt to rig the election. Collins dismissed the demand and said his team had not yet decided whether to appeal.

 Renner is using his closing campaign ads to emphasize his record as House speaker, including the expansion of school-choice programs and conservative legislation passed while he led the chamber. Vote-by-mail ballots have already been distributed for the Aug. 19 primary. Florida's mandatory early-voting period begins Aug. 8 and continues through Aug. 15, though counties may offer additional days. On the Democratic side, David Jolly is already focusing his attacks on Donalds, this week promising to halt new AI data-center construction until Florida develops stronger protections for its water supply, electric grid, communities and consumer privacy.

hero.headline: Two sharks spotted off St. Lucie and Palm Beach County coasts
hero.teaser: A 12-foot shark was hooked by fishermen on Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County on Friday, and a dead hammerhead shark washed up south of the Jupiter Beach Resort the same day.
hero.body:
Two sharks were spotted along the Atlantic Ocean shore on Friday, with video sent to WPBF. Jensen Beach resident Kathy Green was walking along Normandy Beach on Hutchinson Island in St. Lucie County when she filmed a group of fishermen struggling with a 12-foot shark they had hooked. The fishermen unhooked the shark and released it back into the water. Shark expert and conservationist Jim Abernethy believes it was a great white shark by looking at the video.

 Also Friday, a hammerhead shark was spotted dead just south of the Jupiter Beach Resort. Christopher Ray, a musician, submitted video to WPBF. Later that day, Fish Wildlife removed the shark. Shark Week 2026 ran from July 26 to Saturday on the Discovery Channel.

 Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission has ordered Martin County, which also includes Hutchinson Island, to follow rules about people fishing for fish or sharks from the beach or shoreline. Shark fishing requires a state saltwater fishing license to fish within 1,000 feet of the guarded beach boundaries at any time. Under the current county ordinance, shark fishing is prohibited within 1,000 yards of the county's four guarded beaches: Jensen, Stuart, Bathtub and Hobe Sound. On Tuesday, commissioners postponed making a decision and asked attorneys to review the law.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County cities push for more trees and shade as extreme heat bakes neighborhoods
cards.teaser: Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation says the number one need they hear from people, aside from beach access, is shade. Community Greening, a South Florida nonprofit, says adequa
cards.body:
Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation says the number one need they hear from people, aside from beach access, is shade. Community Greening, a South Florida nonprofit, says adequate tree canopy coverage is around the 30 to 40 percent range and virtually every city in Palm Beach County is at least in the 20 percent range and most are lower. The nonprofit has helped plant and give away nearly 30,000 trees across Palm Beach, Broward and parts of Martin County over the past decade.

 Neighborhoods that have adequate tree canopy coverage are on average 7 to 10 degrees cooler than the neighborhoods right next to them that don't have that adequate tree canopy coverage, including at nighttime once the sun is out of the way, according to Josh Weiner, director of communications and engagement for Community Greening. Palm Beach County Parks and Recreation recently partnered with Community Greening to plant 1,000 trees at Dyer Park in West Palm Beach. The county has also started installing additional shade structures, including new coverings over bleachers at Sandalfoot Cove Park in Boca Raton.

 The Resilient Glades Tree Campaign aimed to revitalize tree canopy coverage in South Bay, Belle Glade, Pahokee and Canal Point by planting 2,000 trees at county parks and hosting eight giveaway events. The project was expected to receive roughly $1 million before funding was cut by the Environmental Protection Agency. Community Greening next tree giveaway is scheduled for September at Halpatiokee Regional Park in Martin County. The nonprofit is also partnering with the city of Boca Raton to plant 100 native shade trees along El Rio Trail in September.

cards.headline: Fort Myers man arrested after road rage PIT maneuver crashes family's SUV into fence on I-95 in Martin County
cards.teaser: A Fort Myers man is charged with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and child abuse after deputies say he performed a PIT maneuver on a North Carolina family's vehicle during a road rage incident near Stuart.
cards.body:
Michael Jeffrey Spiers, 36, was arrested Saturday night after he allegedly used a PIT maneuver to send a North Carolina family's SUV into a barbed-wire fence during a road rage attack near Kanner Highway and I-95. The crash happened around 7:30 p.m. Saturday. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident involved a woman traveling alone and her brother, his wife, and their young son following in another vehicle while on vacation from North Carolina.

 Investigators said Spiers first went after the woman, chasing her through a gas station parking lot before following her onto the highway and repeatedly trying to force her off the road. The woman called 911, and Spiers then turned his attention to the family's vehicle. Witnesses reported Spiers was flailing his arms and making what appeared to be gang signs during the encounters.

 Spiers intentionally performed a PIT maneuver on the family's car, sending the SUV spinning off 96th Street near Kanner Highway and crashing into a barbed-wire fence. The three family members ran from the car and hid in the brush until deputies arrived.

 Spiers drove to the nearby Sunoco gas station at Kanner Highway and 96th Street where deputies took him into custody. Deputies found a dog inside Spiers' vehicle that had allegedly been stolen in December from someone Spiers used to date. The dog has been reunited with its owner. Spiers remains jailed on charges of aggravated battery with a deadly weapon, child abuse and reckless driving.

cards.headline: Property tax increases push Treasure Coast resident to relocate to Puerto Rico
cards.teaser: A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives
cards.body:
A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely.

 Tate said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes were going up and he could not afford it anymore.

 His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County.

 Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.

cards.headline: Three candidates vie for Martin County Commission District 4 seat in August 18 primary
cards.teaser: Three candidates are running for the District 4 Martin County Commission seat in the August 18 Primary Election. John Dial, Sarah Heard, and John Kaz Kazanjian qualified for the ra
cards.body:
Three candidates are running for the District 4 Martin County Commission seat in the August 18 Primary Election. John Dial, Sarah Heard, and John Kaz Kazanjian qualified for the race.

 Dial identified over-development as the most serious issue facing Martin County, citing Senate Bill 180, SB102, and new mandates from Tallahassee that remove power from local voters and leaders. He said he would go to Tallahassee as often as necessary to represent local control and push to restore the county's ability to make decisions. Dial also opposed using taxpayer money to fund Brightline, calling it a private company that is not U.S.-owned, carries roughly $2 billion in debt, and is reportedly losing more than $220 million a year. He said he would be open to a train station if a private rail company wanted to invest its own capital, or a fair market land lease at the fairgrounds provided the property would revert to the county if the company fails.

 Heard said the legislature is taking decision-making out of the Board's hands and only essential services like the Sheriff and Fire Rescue can be funded with ad valorem taxes. She said even if funding only public safety, the county would not be able to fund it by the third year. Heard said she is in favor of a train station downtown but would consider the fairgrounds location if the majority of residents overwhelmingly favors it. She said she does not want to see data centers in unincorporated Martin County because they are not allowed uses on agricultural lands, and a comprehensive plan amendment would have to be approved to change the future land use, which she would oppose.

 Both Dial and Heard addressed a potential referendum on raising the Homestead exemption and cutting ad valorem property tax income. Dial said he would protect essential services first including fire protection, law enforcement, waste management, and education while reviewing non-essential programs and discretionary spending for reductions. He also suggested exploring ways to turn costly county assets like Sailfish Splash, the golf course, and the cafe on the beach into revenue-producing opportunities by leasing them to private operators.

 On the Business Development Board's annual $450,000 funding, which District 1 Commissioner Eileen Vargas opposed on June 23, Dial said he supports the BDB in its current role but that every use of taxpayer dollars must be examined carefully if spending cuts are forced. Heard agreed that the BDB is too dependent on government funding.

cards.headline: Martin County REACH Center launches workforce training programs in aviation, healthcare, and manufacturing
cards.teaser: Martin County's REACH Center has opened its doors and begun offering workforce training programs designed to prepare residents for jobs in high-demand industries. The roughly $4.5
cards.body:
Martin County's REACH Center has opened its doors and begun offering workforce training programs designed to prepare residents for jobs in high-demand industries. The roughly $4.5 million facility completed construction earlier this year and is now hosting courses ranging from medical administrative assistant certification to technical aviation training for Daher Aerospace.

 Evelyn Lopez was among the first 10 students to complete a medical administrative assistant cohort this summer. She passed the certification exam and is now exploring job opportunities. The program included mock interviews with professionals to prepare students for the hiring process. Lopez said her parents were proud of her achievement because it opened more career opportunities.

 George Stokus, assistant county administrator, said the center serves students uncertain about college, those without financial means to pursue higher education immediately, and adults seeking career changes or skill improvements. The facility aims to create a local pipeline for jobs in aviation, marine, medicine, manufacturing, and environmental studies.

 Ted Astolfi, CEO and president of the Economic Council of Martin County, said the center's mission focuses on creating upward economic mobility for the community. The center aims to help residents grow into better jobs rather than remain at a single economic level. Additional programs are planned to expand the range of training opportunities available to Martin County residents.

hero.headline: Driver sought after hitting two children and fleeing scene in Fort Pierce
hero.teaser: The Fort Pierce Police Department is searching for a driver who struck two children with a car on Saturday and left the scene before authorities arrived.
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department is searching for a driver who struck two children with a car on Saturday and left the scene before authorities arrived. The crash happened on 25th Street near the Elks Lodge in Fort Pierce.

Investigators said the driver, believed to be between 20 and 30 years old, stopped briefly to check on the children after the crash but then drove away. Police are looking for a gold Mercedes-Benz that may have damage to the driver's side.

One of the children was taken to a hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The condition of the second child has not been released.

Anyone with information about the driver or the vehicle is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County schools open Aug. 10 with new Tradition Lakes K-8 campus and AI courses
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Public Schools will open for students on Aug. 10 with enrollment expected to hold steady at 42,505 students, though the district is adding new facilities and progr
cards.body:
Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County is set to open its doors on Aug. 10, offering classroom space for one of the county's fastest-growing communities. Crews have worked throughout the summer to prepare the campus for its first group of students. Principal Latanya Greene said the school's motto, 'Traditions begin here,' reflects the focus on building a foundation of achievements and accomplishments.

The new campus comes at a critical time for the Tradition area, where population growth has led to overcrowding at nearby schools. District leaders expect as many as 1,600 students on opening day, with many families benefiting from the school's convenient location. 'We are busting at the seams in the south and the west. And this school is so conveniently located to families that we're going to have a tremendous number of students that are walking or even other parents dropping the kids off in a golf cart,' said John R. Prince, superintendent of St. Lucie County Public Schools.

Greene emphasized that months of planning have gone into creating an environment where students can grow academically and socially. 'It's about being in an environment that you can grow and continue with great levels. But bigger than that, you begin to set the tone of creating those strong academics that move with you from year to year to year. You develop friendships,' Greene said.

cards.headline: Property tax increases push Treasure Coast resident to relocate to Puerto Rico

cards.body:
A Treasure Coast man said rising property taxes in Florida pushed him to leave the state and buy a home in Puerto Rico, where he pays nothing in property taxes. Jock Tate now lives in Salinas, Puerto Rico, in a 3-bedroom home he purchased for $95,000. As a disabled veteran, he qualifies for exemptions that eliminate his property tax bill entirely.

 Tate said the price of housing in Puerto Rico is much less than Florida, especially South Florida. He said property taxes were going up and he could not afford it anymore.

 His move comes as Florida homeowners face rising property tax burdens across the state. According to a Florida Tax Watch study, property taxes rose 146.2% in St. Lucie County between 2014 and 2024. Other Treasure Coast counties saw similar increases: 131.5% in Okeechobee County, 99.4% in Palm Beach County, 90.1% in Indian River County and 90.1% in Martin County.

 Florida voters will have a chance to weigh in on property taxes this November. A referendum on the ballot would raise the Homestead Exemption, lowering property tax bills for Florida homeowners. Many city and county officials have warned that rolling back property taxes would lead to budget cuts and force local governments to raise other fees and taxes to offset lost revenue.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce gets 90-day extension to pay state fines for Little Jim's dock violations
cards.teaser: The Florida Department of Environmental Protection extended the city's deadline to Sept. 15 to review a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle.
cards.body:
The Florida Department of Environmental Protection gave Fort Pierce until Sept. 15 to review, approve and submit a proposed consent order resolving nearly $16,000 in state fines tied to docks at Little Jim Bait & Tackle. The state agency extended the city's deadline by 90 days, meaning city commissioners have not yet formally accepted or rejected the state's enforcement terms. City staff have been negotiating with FDEP to reduce or resolve the thousands of dollars in penalties.

 The enforcement action follows allegations that the city has been operating docks at Little Jim's on state-owned submerged land without authorization. FDEP says the city never had permission to use the land. City Commissioner Michael Broderick acknowledged the allegation on July 6.

 The FDEP action is one of several legal and regulatory pressures surrounding the historic waterfront property. In early July, Fort Pierce city commissioners voted unanimously to reject a settlement offer in a lawsuit filed by local resident Kevin Keene, who alleged years of waterfront mismanagement tied to Little Jim's. The city has filed a motion to dismiss Keene's amended complaint.

 Keene said he will continue to pursue litigation. Broderick said the city is planning to hire a real estate manager to oversee development decisions and prevent future situations.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.teaser: Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a domestic violence incident at her Port St.
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a domestic violence incident at her Port St. Lucie residence on Saturday, Aug. 2. Her partner, Ralph Varela Sr., 50, shot her with an AR-style rifle before taking his own life, according to Port St. Lucie police.

 Officers responded around 7:40 p.m. to the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace, west of U.S. 1 and near HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital, after receiving multiple 911 calls reporting gunshots and a domestic disturbance. Investigators determined that Ortega and Varela had been in a long-term cohabitation relationship and were in the process of separating. Their adult son had left the residence to pick up dinner when Varela began shooting Ortega inside the home.

 Surveillance video shows Ortega attempting to flee into the front yard while Varela continued firing before she collapsed. She was airlifted to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Officers later found Varela dead inside the home from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.

 Ortega began her emergency communications career with the Greenacres Police Department in November 2001. When the Greenacres Police Department and its communications unit merged with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in February 2016, she continued her work there. The sheriff's office said Ortega was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion and a warm smile. Her son, Ralph Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue.

 According to Palm Beach Clerk records, Varela Sr. was convicted in 2014 of discharging a firearm in public and sentenced to 192 days in jail. In 2017, he was convicted of possession of cocaine, reckless driving, driving while his license was not active and refusal to submit to a chemical or physical test, and was sentenced to 20 days in jail. The investigation remains active as detectives continue processing evidence and await the final results from the Medical Examiner's Office.

cards.headline: Honduran national convicted in Fort Pierce federal court for firearms trafficking to Honduras
cards.teaser: A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them
cards.body:
A federal jury in Fort Pierce convicted a Honduran national for operating a firearms-trafficking network that purchased guns in South Florida through straw buyers and smuggled them to Honduras. Luis Matute Figueroa, 33, of Lake Worth, was found guilty of conspiracy and possession of a firearm by an illegal alien, the U.S. Department of Justice announced Monday.

 Matute Figueroa overstayed a tourist visa in 2017 and remained in the United States without lawful status. WhatsApp messages recovered during the investigation showed that Matute Figueroa provided co-conspirators with firearm inventories, pricing information and shipping instructions for weapons destined for Honduras. The messages also contained a photograph and a video of Matute Figueroa in possession of a distinctive gold Colt 1911 pistol. U.S. Attorney Markenzy Lapointe said the defendant exploited his unlawful presence in the United States to help traffic American firearms to Honduras.

 Court records and trial evidence showed that Matute Figueroa conspired with Gerson Eliu Padilla-Figueroa, Juan Matute Figueroa, Ariel Henriquez-Padilla, and William Mendoza to acquire firearms in the United States through straw purchases and illegally export them to Honduras. Straw purchases involve using individuals with clean records to buy firearms on behalf of those prohibited from owning them.

 Matute Figueroa faces up to five years in federal prison on the conspiracy count and up to 15 years in prison on the firearm possession count. A federal district court judge will determine the sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. The ATF Miami Field Office and Homeland Security Investigations Miami investigated the case with assistance from the Broward Sheriff's Office, the Martin County Sheriff's Office, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection. Attorney Suzanne Huyler is prosecuting the case.

hero.headline: Vero Beach keeps millage flat at 2.98 mills, adds $410,000 to budget for police positions
hero.teaser: The Vero Beach City Council set a preliminary millage rate for the 2026-27 fiscal year at the current 2.9816 mills during a July 22 budget workshop, approving a $37,352,589 budget
hero.body:
The Vero Beach City Council set a preliminary millage rate for the 2026-27 fiscal year at the current 2.9816 mills during a July 22 budget workshop, approving a $37,352,589 budget that includes $410,000 transferred from the General Fund's unassigned fund balance to cover salaries for three vacant police officer positions. City Manager Monte Falls told the council the city holds a strong financial position with a total General Fund balance of $54 million, including $17.7 million in unassigned funds and $35.56 million in committed reserves.

 Falls recommended using $435,160 from the unassigned balance to offset the city's Other Post Employee Benefit trust payment, which would allow the vacant police positions to be filled. For a Vero Beach homeowner with a property assessed at $300,000, a $50,000 Homestead Exemption and a Save Our Homes 3 percent increase, the current millage rate would result in about $25 a year in additional ad valorem tax, Falls said.

 Vice Mayor Linda Moore and Councilmember Taylor Dingle raised concerns about funding recurring positions with non-recurring money, particularly with Amendment 3 on the November ballot potentially creating a $1.3 million budget hole. Mayor John Cotugno said Vero Beach would fare better than other Florida communities if Amendment 3 passes because the city has four enterprise funds and a diversified tax base including industrial, residential and commercial revenue sources.

 After debate, the council approved adding the $410,000 to the budget by offsetting capital expenses already included in the operating budget. Falls told Hometown News on Sept. 27 that the new police officer salaries would actually cost the city an extra $300,000. The council will return in September to set the final millage rate and adopt the budget.

cards.headline: Space Coast Symphony Orchestra brings Landscapes & Legends concert to Vero Beach
cards.teaser: The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra will perform Landscapes Legends on Sunday, August 10, at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street. The concert features works explori
cards.body:
The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra will perform Landscapes Legends on Sunday, August 10, at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street. The concert features works exploring magic and myth, with guest conductor Patrick Phillips leading the performance.

 The program opens with Dukas' The Sorcerer's Apprentice, the 11-minute orchestral tone poem famously depicted in Disney's Fantasia. The concert includes the world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs' Cloud Slant, a work capturing light, motion and atmosphere. Fuchs won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium for an album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos.

 Vero Beach music and arts leader Dr. Jacob Craig will perform Edward MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive three-movement work composed in 1885. The work holds the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist Van Cliburn chose MacDowell's Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut.

 The concert concludes with Pines of Rome, the 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer Ottorino Respighi. The 22-minute work dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Tickets cost $35 through www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches, and $40 at the door.

 Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free. For more information, call 855-252-7276.

cards.headline: Senior Resource Association and FPL deliver hurricane meal kits to Indian River County seniors
cards.teaser: Florida Power Light Company partnered with Senior Resource Association to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County as the Atlantic hurricane season continues.
cards.body:
Senior Resource Association worked with Florida Power Light Company to distribute hurricane preparedness meal kits to seniors in Indian River County during the six-month Atlantic hurricane season. The effort, also in partnership with the Florida Council on Aging, provides vital supplies to vulnerable seniors in the communities the companies serve.

 Each kit includes three days of shelf-stable food, water and snacks for seniors who may not be able to leave their homes or receive home-delivered meals immediately after a storm. The kits also include a hurricane preparedness guide with tips and resources. Volunteers from FPL and SRA distributed the kits to help ensure seniors have the resources they need to stay safe.

 Senior Resource Association President and CEO Karen Deigl said FPL has been an incredible partner to the organization. FPL External Affairs Manager Michele Murrell said the company is committed to ensuring vulnerable customers have the necessary resources to weather any storm. FPL has worked with local community nonprofits to deliver thousands of hurricane kits to help seniors prepare for storm season since 2016.

cards.headline: Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board recommends Miracle Mile extension for former Doctors Clinic site
cards.teaser: The Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board unanimously recommended the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel at 2300 5th Ave. from residential to commercial for mixed-use development.
cards.body:
The Vero Beach Planning & Zoning Board unanimously recommended July 16 that the City Council change the land use of a seven-acre parcel from residential to commercial so a developer can repurpose the property at 2300 5th Ave. for mixed-use development as part of a northern extension of the Miracle Mile Business District. The applicant, 2300 5th Avenue LLC, has purchased an office building known locally as the Doctors Clinic. Through redevelopment, the site is planned to become integrated into the Miracle Mile area.

 Principal Planner Cheri Fitzgerald said the request would change the future land use map from residential medium to commercial. The property is currently an office and pre-school. The amendment would extend the Miracle Mile commercial district to the north, which would allow mixed-use residential and commercial uses that could better align with more recent development trends. Fitzgerald based her recommendation of approval on the application's compliance with city code.

 Contracted Land Planner Rebecca Grohall said the site was originally the Doctors Clinic specialized in healthcare, but many specialty medical practices eventually migrated toward the hospital. Today, it is generally utilized as office and a pre-school and faces vacancy rates and under-utilization. Grohall said the site plan has not been started because the Commercial Land Use designation is needed first.

 Possibilities include a hotel, multifamily units, and a true mixed-use development with ground-floor retail and upper floor residential uses. The Planning & Zoning Board voted 4-0 to recommend approval.

cards.headline: Indian River County Commission District 2 candidates outline priorities ahead of Aug. 18 primary
cards.teaser: Four candidates for the Indian River County Commission District 2 seat answered questions on issues ranging from property tax reform to affordable housing and agricultural land preservation.
cards.body:
The Hometown News sent the same list of questions to each qualified candidate in the Aug. 18 Republican Primary Election for the District 2 Indian River County Commission seat. The only qualified Democratic candidate in the race also agreed to participate, although he will not face the winner of the primary until November. Candidates answered questions about the most serious issue facing Indian River County, a referendum on raising the Homestead Exemption and potentially cutting ad valorem property tax income, affordable housing, rezoning of agricultural lands, and improving quality of life.

 Republican candidate Bob McPartlan, who served 15 years on the Sebastian City Council, said the most serious issue is managing growth in a way that protects quality of life, infrastructure and the Indian River Lagoon. He does not support the property tax amendment as written, saying it was developed quickly without a full analysis of its impact. Republican candidate Jennifer Pippin said if the amendment passes, she would begin by evaluating discretionary spending, including $3.7 million in funding provided to non-profit organizations and the $1.4 million budget for school resource officers currently paid by the county. Republican candidate Daniel Brooks Robinson said the greatest challenge is managing growth responsibly and ensuring roads, utilities, public safety and infrastructure keep pace.

 Democratic candidate Robert (Robbie) D. Hardingham said the Indian River Lagoon is one of the most serious issues facing the county. He said the stormwater runoff and pollution from nitrates, phosphorus and algae blooms are causing an ecological disaster.

 He said the septic-to-sewer initiative will help but solutions are needed to speed up the cleaning of the Lagoon. Hardingham said he hopes the property tax referendum will not pass because it will be bad for schools, businesses and renters.

cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is attempting to locate Kaden Joseph Simon, a 24-year-old man who was last seen leaving his residence around 2:30 p.m. on Tuesday. Simon was wearing black pants, a black shirt and flip-flop sandals when he left. His direction of travel was unknown.

 Simon has brown hair and brown eyes, stands at 5-foot-7, and weighs 160 pounds. The sheriff's office announced the search for Simon on Tuesday.

 Anyone with information regarding his whereabouts is asked to contact Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers at 1-800-273-8477. The sheriff's office did not release additional information about the circumstances surrounding his disappearance.

 The Indian River County Sheriff's Office is located in Indian River County, which includes Vero Beach, Sebastian, and Fellsmere.
